narrative:
The model predicted a 56% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability tipped above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your LSAT score had the strongest influence and pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. At 20, it sits far below the average of 37 among students who were accepted, signaling weaker preparation in the skills the bar exam tests. Your first-year law school grades came next in importance and also worked against you. Placing in the bottom decile (1 out of 10) compared with an average of 6 among accepted students told the model you struggled early in the program. Your undergraduate GPA was the third most important factor, but it actually pulled the prediction slightly in the positive direction. At 3.10 it is only modestly below the 3.23 average of accepted students, so the model saw some underlying academic ability.

Taken together, the low LSAT and weak early law school performance outweighed the decent college record and led the system to forecast a failing outcome.

You should focus on strengthening the areas the model weighed most heavily. Retaking the LSAT and aiming for a substantially higher score, combined with a clear plan to improve your law school grades, would most directly improve your chances on a future application. Consider full-time study and targeted bar-prep resources before reapplying.
